content: The blower is powered by the engine to deliver an air volume of approximately 1000–1500 m³/hour. When a nozzle is attached to the end of the air discharge tube, it emits 750 m³/hour ± 5% at a velocity of approximately 100 m/s. The blower and engine combination must operate at a single maximum or optimal speed, as reducing the engine speed will compromise the atomization required for producing a fine mist spray. The air from the blower is directed through a flexible duct to the nozzle, allowing the operator to adjust the spray direction. The spray tank is typically slightly pressurized by channeling air from the fan into the tank, ensuring consistent delivery of the spray to the nozzle. The flow rate is influenced by the height of the nozzle relative to the liquid level in the tank. A pump may be installed to ensure the spray liquid is delivered from the pesticide tank to the nozzle without being affected by the liquid level in the tank. A 50-mesh or finer filter must be placed in the liquid flow line to prevent blockages in the nozzle or restrictor. The liquid spray flow rate to the nozzle is regulated by pre-selected restrictors positioned inline before the nozzle. The air velocity must remain constant during application, as variations can alter droplet size. The liquid spray delivery to the nozzle is controlled by an on/off valve located on the air duct in front of the operator. An air shear or rotary atomizer can be installed at the end of the air delivery tube to produce droplets with a volume median diameter (VMD) in the range of 50–100 µm. Some mist blowers are equipped with very low flow rate restrictors that produce droplets with a VMD of less than 50 µm, suitable for space spraying. However, these small restrictors are prone to blockages if the pesticide formulation contains large particulate matter. When operated at the recommended engine speed, the sprayer should project droplets at least 10 meters horizontally and 6 meters vertically in still air. There should be at least five droplets per cm² to indicate the maximum distance the droplets were projected. The sprayer must undergo a minimum of 50 hours of operation over a 10-day period, including one 8-hour session to simulate a full day’s operation in a vector-borne disease outbreak area. All stoppages must be recorded, along with the reasons and details of any repairs. Fuel consumption data must also be collected. If the noise level exceeds 85 decibels near the operator’s ear, the equipment must be permanently labeled to indicate the need for ear protection. The sprayer must be equipped with a twoor four-stroke engine weighing less than 12 kg. A positive displacement reciprocating pump capable of delivering up to 10 L/min at 6 bar pressure must be installed, although it will typically operate at lower flow rates and pressures. The tank capacity must be at least 10 liters and made of materials compatible with the specified pesticide products. A trigger valve with a positive lock-off position must be included, with a lever length of at least 100 mm from the pivot point. Filters must be installed to prevent nozzle blockages, with at least one filter positioned close to the nozzle. The lance attached to the trigger valve must be at least 500 mm long and fitted with a control flow valve to ensure a constant spray flow rate, compensating for variations in pump speed. The nozzle tip and flow rate must comply with international standards (ISO 10625:2005). Portable cold foggers, either hand-carried or knapsack-mounted, are used for space treatment in buildings, houses, and outdoor areas inaccessible to vehicles. These devices must have an engine with an easy-start mechanism. Electrically powered units for indoor use must meet the same requirements for spray tank and droplet size. For engine-driven cold foggers, the fuel tank must be mounted below the engine, and engine controls, including a stop switch, must be visible to the operator. The engine/blower unit must be mounted on a knapsack frame designed for comfortable carrying, with vibration-dampening features and a non-absorbent padded backrest. All adjustable parts must be permanently and clearly marked. The fuel tank capacity must allow at least one hour of field operation without stopping the engine. The pesticide tank must have a capacity of at least 1 liter, with a clear gauge to indicate the liquid volume. If the tank is pressurized above 50 kPa, a device to completely depressurize the tank before opening must be provided. The blower must provide sufficient air volume and velocity to atomize the spray liquid and project the cold fog droplets away from the operator. A vortical nozzle must shear the spray into droplets with a VMD of less than 30 µm at the recommended output for waterand oil-based formulations. A liquid cut-off valve is required to stop the fogging treatment at any time. Vehicle-mounted cold foggers are aerosol-generating machines mounted on flatbed trucks, trailers, boats, amphibious vehicles, or drones. These are used for outdoor space treatments requiring no residual spray deposit. The equipment must be mounted on a corrosion-resistant frame and include a pesticide tank and an additional tank for flushing the system. A control system operable from the vehicle cabin must be provided, along with a fuel tank sufficient for at least two hours of operation. All tanks must be permanently marked and equipped with drainage facilities. The engine exhaust and moving parts must be guarded to prevent injury, and the engine must have a timer (hour meter). Manually carried thermal foggers, primarily used for space spray treatments in buildings and outdoor areas inaccessible to vehicles, must have a thermal energy nozzle to atomize the insecticide liquid into droplets of the desired size. These devices must include a battery starting mechanism, a manual or battery-operated air pump for pressurizing the fuel line, a handle for safe carrying, and a robust frame to hold the components. All hot surfaces must be adequately guarded to prevent burns, and all adjustable parts must be permanently marked.
